sections.html:
Tumwater lies in Thurston County, roughly two miles south of Olympia at the spot where the Deschutes River empties into Budd Inlet. The middle-priced owned home is worth $472,200, and owners live in 62.5 percent of Tumwater homes. The population climbed from 17,371 in 2010 to 25,350 in 2020 and is now estimated at 28,010, up 7.6 percent from 2020.

Median household income is $95,212 and commutes average 21.3 minutes. Few people move within the city. A year earlier, 85.8 percent of residents were in the very same house, so sellers are often longtime owners with a long history of repairs and permits.

sections.h2: Older homes and the falls district
sections.html:
The city bills itself as the Oregon Trail's endpoint and Puget Sound's oldest lasting American settlement. Settlers arrived at Tumwater Falls in 1845, and incorporation came on November 25, 1869. The Tumwater Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978, preserves what was left of downtown after Interstate 5 opened in 1958 and about 100 buildings came down.

Own an older place, or one near the falls? Phone Community Development at (360) 754-4180 to find out if a local historic listing or critical area rule affects the lot, ideally before a buyer's agent raises it.

The Tumwater Municipal Code governs building, remodeling and new construction, and the Building Division enforces it. That office also reviews plans and inspects for building and fire code, and a Development Review Committee weighs whether a project can go forward.

A few steps help before you list:

  • Locate permits for anything you added or replaced since buying: a deck, a finished basement, a furnace.
  • For a permit that was never finished, the Building Division can explain how to close it. Platting and planned unit development questions go to that same number, (360) 754-4180.
  • Look up your zoning in the city's building codes and development guide.
  • Check the Development Projects map for construction near your street.

A buyer's inspector often catches unpermitted work, and an open permit may delay closing. Fix it while you still set the pace.

sections.h2: Flood and drainage on low lots
sections.html:
Thurston County has urged residents to prepare for fall and winter flooding from major rivers, heavy rain, saturated soils, rising groundwater and overwhelmed drainage systems. The city is also asking residents to mark places on an interactive map where more attention is needed for climate resilience planning.

If your lot is near the river or in a low spot, ask the city what that map shows and whether any flood or drainage rule applies. Buyers who see standing water in a photo will ask the same question, and a short written answer from the city is better than a guess. Keep any drainage fixes and records with the permit file.

Thurston County's Treasurer bills Tumwater parcels. Visit 3000 Pacific Ave SE in Olympia on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., or call 360-786-5550.

The annual bill comes in two installments, April 30 and October 31, and a weekend due date slides to the next business day. You can pay online, at the counter, in the drop box out front or by mail. Mail early, because same-day postmarks are no longer guaranteed.

Find out from the Treasurer if your parcel owes anything, so the title company can deduct it from what you receive.

sections.h2: Excise tax and the disclosure form
sections.html:
Do not confuse property tax with the excise tax charged on the sale itself. That second tax usually falls on the seller, goes to the treasurer of the county where the land lies, and is due when the sale occurs. If nobody pays, a lien attaches to the property, and after a month interest begins. State rates run 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 and 1.28 percent through $1,525,000, plus a local portion.

Washington's RCW 64.06.020 sets a seller disclosure form with questions on the roof, foundation, plumbing, electrical system, heating, drainage and more. Buyers of most homes should have it within five business days after contract signing. A line on the form also notes the carbon monoxide alarm and smoke detection requirement. The statute shows the full form.

Cash suits a house in rough shape or a seller in a hurry. The buyer takes the property as is, and with no bank involved there is no appraisal or repair demand to derail things.

Stack a cash price against a listing using these yardsticks:

  • Money left after commission, repairs and holding costs.
  • Whether the closing date matches your move.
  • Who is responsible for excise tax, title and recording fees.
  • How the buyer treats an open permit, a tenant or leftover belongings.

Insist on a written offer. Before signing, have a Thurston County title or escrow company confirm the payoff and walk you through the deed process.

Begin with paperwork: the tax statement, permit records and anything still open. Then phone the Building Division about unfinished work and the Treasurer about a balance. Armed with those answers, you can weigh a listing against a cash sale using real figures.

Listing brings showings, buyer financing and an appraisal. Selling for cash brings a written offer, a title review and a closing date you negotiate. Either way, the disclosure statement is owed inside five business days of signing, so complete it candidly and keep a copy.

Known problems, including unpermitted work, belong on the form. Disclosing them up front is cheaper than a dispute after closing.

At closing, the title or escrow officer clears any mortgage, delinquent property tax or lien and remits the excise tax to the county treasurer. Recording the deed finishes the sale. A payoff higher than you expected is much easier to handle in the week before closing, so confirm balances with the Treasurer early.

Gather permit records and any warranties for work done on the house so the buyer receives them with the keys. Also settle in advance which fixtures and equipment stay. Walk through the house with the buyer's agent or the cash buyer so nothing is assumed. If a tenant or stored items remain, agree on a move-out date in writing, since a cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands still needs to know what condition it will be in on closing day.

faqs.q: How many people live in Tumwater?
faqs.a: The latest estimate is 28,010, compared with 25,350 in 2020 and 17,371 in 2010.

faqs.q: Which county handles property tax in Tumwater?
faqs.a: The county Treasurer, reachable at 360-786-5550 or at the Olympia office on Pacific Ave SE. Half the year's tax is due each spring and fall, so ask about any balance before you close.

faqs.q: Who pays real estate excise tax when a Tumwater house sells?
faqs.a: Normally the seller, paid to the county treasurer when the sale closes. Unpaid tax can become a lien on the house, and a local portion is added to the state rate that starts at 1.1 percent.

faqs.q: Do I need permits closed before selling a Tumwater house?
faqs.a: It is a good idea. Contact the Building Division at (360) 754-4180 about permits for additions or major systems, and keep the records for the buyer.
The city calls itself the oldest permanent American settlement on Puget Sound and the end of the Oregon Trail. It sits at Tumwater Falls and was incorporated in 1869.
